title: Significance inflation
guidance:
**Tell:** Ordinary details are called pivotal, profound, timeless, legendary,
transformative, or representative of a broader shift.

**Repair:** Name the concrete change and its consequence.

**Boundary:** Bare *in the evolution of* is ordinary English. The inflation
shape needs an inflating word immediately before it (*chapter*, *milestone*,
*role*, *turning point*); neutral scientific and historical uses stay clean.
(Adapted from avoid-ai-writing v3.37.0 post-release tip, MIT.)

title: Genre-register drift
guidance:
**Tell:** Stock genre language replaces the vocabulary of the actual world,
profession, publication, or speaker.

**Repair:** Use named practices, materials, institutions, tools, and stakes.

title: Corporate and motivational register
guidance:
**Tell:** Words such as *impactful*, *empower*, *leverage*, *optimize*,
*meaningful*, *deeply*, or *genuinely* replace a specific action or result.

**Repair:** State who did what and what changed.

title: Imported psychological vocabulary
guidance:
**Tell:** A narrator or character uses therapeutic or diagnostic language that
does not fit the speaker, period, genre, or evidence.

**Repair:** Render observed behavior, sensation, memory, and choice. Keep exact
clinical terms when the context requires them.

title: Promotional language
guidance:
**Tell:** Neutral prose sounds like a brochure through words such as *vibrant*,
*renowned*, *stunning*, *groundbreaking*, *thriving*, or *world-class*.

**Repair:** Replace praise with a fact the reader can evaluate.

title: Abstract noun preference
guidance:
**Tell:** *Community*, *resilience*, *innovation*, *culture*, *hope*,
*transformation*, or *impact* carries the sentence without a visible act or object.

**Repair:** Show the exchange, decision, object, or outcome that supports the
abstraction.

title: Em-dash cluster
guidance:
**Tell:** Dashes manufacture drama, rhythm, or parenthetical depth several times
in one passage.

**Repair:** Keep a dash for a real interruption or turn. Use a period, comma,
colon, or reordered sentence elsewhere. Dash frequency is a style judgment,
never an authorship signal: upstream scores it at zero weight for the same
reason the house rule already states below.

title: Rule-of-three padding
guidance:
**Tell:** Claims, adjectives, or examples arrive in polished triads because three
sounds complete.

**Repair:** Keep the number of points the content earns. One precise detail often
beats three generic ones.

title: Negative-then-positive clarification
guidance:
**Tell:** Repeated *It is not X. It is Y.* and *X rather than Y* constructions
manufacture emphasis or sophistication without sharpening the distinction. The
same move hides at larger scales: a split-sentence contrast (*This does not
mean every choice is equal. It means no system confirms which is right.*), a
multi-negation countdown stacking several rejections before the reveal (*It is
not the price. It is not the features. It is the trust.*), and a clipped
negative tail tacked onto a sentence (*The options come from the selected
item, no guessing.*).

**Repair:** State the claim directly or make the contrast factual. Cut a
countdown straight to the positive claim. Write a clipped tail as a real
clause (*without forcing the user to guess*) or cut it.

**Carve-outs:** Keep a contrast when the negative half corrects a belief the
reader actually holds, when it carries the argument, or when both halves carry
information. When the positive claim is not supplied, report the empty contrast
instead of inventing a differentiator; repetition alone does not authorize
removing a contrast with content. Negations
enumerating spec constraints in a list (*no dependencies, no telemetry*) are
list content, not a reveal. (Split-sentence, countdown, and tail forms adapted
from avoid-ai-writing v3.33.0 and blader/humanizer v3.0.0, MIT. Contrast
carve-out extended from the avoid-ai-writing post-v3.38.0 tip, MIT.)

title: Copula avoidance
guidance:
**Tell:** *Serves as*, *stands as*, *functions as*, *represents*, *boasts*, or
*offers* replaces *is* or *has*.

**Repair:** Prefer the plain verb unless the substitute adds meaning.

**Boundary:** *Features* is a copula substitute only as a verb ("the app
features a dashboard", "This Windows 11 app features support for dark mode").
The plural noun is ordinary product writing, so "three new features", a
*Features* heading, "we ship features", counted subjects ("The two platform
features"), and partitives ("All of the system features") stay clean. A year
or version in the product name does not make the subject plural.
(Adapted from avoid-ai-writing v3.37.0 post-release tip, MIT.)

title: Elegant variation and repeated openings
guidance:
**Tell:** Synonyms rotate to avoid repeating the correct name, technical term, or
role. Related: several consecutive sentences open on the same subject, often
*she* or *he*, because each sentence restarts from zero instead of joining the
one before it.

**Repair:** Repeat the right word; consistency is clearer than decorative
variation. For repeated openings, merge the sentences, change the subject when
that helps, or open on the action. Fix the repeated sentence pattern, not the
word: the repaired sentence may still start with *She*. Keep deliberate
repetition that builds rhythm or pressure, as in *She came. She saw. She
conquered.* (Extension adapted from blader/humanizer, MIT.)

title: Hedging stack
guidance:
**Tell:** *Perhaps*, *possibly*, *arguably*, *somewhat*, *in some ways*, and *to
an extent* accumulate until the sentence makes no usable claim.

**Repair:** Keep only uncertainty supported by the evidence.

title: Gerund opening
guidance:
**Tell:** Paragraphs start with static retrospective phrases such as *Having
worked on...*, *Knowing that...*, or *Feeling the weight...*.

**Repair:** Open on the action, observation, or claim that moves the passage.

title: Balanced compound conclusion
guidance:
**Tell:** A paragraph ends on a polished balance such as challenge and
opportunity, fear and hope, or old and new.

**Repair:** Land on the fact, consequence, image, or next decision.

title: Trailing qualifier
guidance:
**Tell:** A sentence gives final emphasis to *for the most part*, *as best they
could*, *to a degree*, or *where possible*.

**Repair:** Move necessary qualification earlier or end on the hard fact.

title: Not-just-X-but-Y construction
guidance:
**Tell:** *Not just X, but Y* repeatedly signals nuance or escalation without
adding evidence.

**Repair:** State the stronger claim directly and support it.

**Carve-outs:** Keep a contrast that carries the argument or corrects a real
misconception, and retain both supplied propositions when simplifying a frame,
including a stated value judgment. Repetition alone does not authorize removal.
Never invent a differentiator to fill an empty second half. (Adapted from the
avoid-ai-writing post-v3.38.0 tip, MIT.)

title: Topic-sentence paragraph
guidance:
**Tell:** Every paragraph announces its subject, supplies examples, and closes
with a summary.

**Repair:** Start where the thought becomes useful and stop when it has done its
work.

title: Continuity bridge sentence
guidance:
**Tell:** *Furthermore*, *building on this*, *against this backdrop*, or *with
that in mind* exists only to connect neighboring paragraphs.

**Repair:** Cut the bridge. Reorder the paragraphs if the connection remains
unclear.

title: Thematic restatement ending
guidance:
**Tell:** The final sentence explains what the preceding scene or passage meant.

**Repair:** End on the evidence and trust the reader to infer the theme.

title: Even-rhythm paragraph
guidance:
**Tell:** Sentences share the same length, cadence, and grammatical shape.

**Repair:** Let sentence length follow thought. Use short sentences for hard
turns and longer ones for connected reasoning.

title: Signposting sentence
guidance:
**Tell:** *It is important to note*, *the key point is*, *here is what matters*,
or *let's dive in* announces emphasis before delivering content. The casual
register counts too: *heads up*, *quick note*, *before I forget*, or *one thing
that bit me, so pay attention to this part* announces the point instead of
making it. Remove the announcement, not just its formal tone.

**Repair:** Begin with the important content.

title: Backstory dump on first mention
guidance:
**Tell:** A person, place, product, or institution arrives with a complete
history before the present action can continue.

**Repair:** Introduce what matters now. Reveal history when it changes the
reader's understanding or a character's choice.

title: Emotion announcement
guidance:
**Tell:** The narrator names emotion instead of rendering what a person notices,
does, or cannot do.

**Repair:** Use bodily response, attention, gesture, and choice when useful. Keep
a direct emotion word when blunt self-naming suits the voice.

title: Sympathetic narrator insert
guidance:
**Tell:** *Little did she know*, *fate had other plans*, or *things were about to
change* reassures, foreshadows, or explains from outside the scene.

**Repair:** Remove the intrusion or foreshadow through a concrete detail.

title: Over-explained motivation
guidance:
**Tell:** The narrator supplies a full reason for each action rather than letting
behavior, context, or prior events carry it.

**Repair:** Show the choice and enough evidence for the reader to infer why.

title: Analytical self-awareness
guidance:
**Tell:** A first-person narrator perfectly diagnoses their own defenses,
projections, motives, and emotional substitutions.

**Repair:** Match the speaker's plausible self-knowledge. Let gaps and
contradictions remain when they belong to the voice.

title: Explanatory memory flashback
guidance:
**Tell:** A memory arrives exactly when needed to explain the present emotion or
deliver backstory.

**Repair:** Keep memory fragmentary and triggered by a specific sensation,
object, phrase, or action.

title: Expressive dialogue tag
guidance:
**Tell:** A tag adds a clause such as *her voice heavy with sorrow* or *his words
carrying authority*.

**Repair:** Use *said*, *asked*, no tag, or an action beat. Put emotion in the line
and situation.

title: Dialogue that explains shared backstory
guidance:
**Tell:** Characters tell each other facts they both know so the reader can catch
up.

**Repair:** Give the question to someone who lacks the information, or reveal it
through disagreement, action, or consequence.

title: Perfect grammar in all speech
guidance:
**Tell:** Every speaker uses complete, polished sentences and the same register.

**Repair:** Distinguish speakers through cadence, vocabulary, omission, and what
each assumes. Avoid cartoon dialect and random errors.

title: Dialogue tags used for emotion
guidance:
**Tell:** Characters constantly hiss, bark, scoff, groan, exclaim, or stammer.

**Repair:** Use a marked tag only when the sound or act matters. Otherwise use
*said* or an action beat.

title: Character who summarizes for the reader
guidance:
**Tell:** A character recaps the plot, argument, or problem in a polished list.

**Repair:** Let the reader assemble the situation. If a recap is necessary, make
it serve a real action.

title: Generic atmospheric opener
guidance:
**Tell:** A scene starts with free-floating weather, darkness, silence, or mood.

**Repair:** Anchor atmosphere to a body, tool, task, or decision.

title: Over-complete information
guidance:
**Tell:** The draft answers every likely question and inventories every aspect of
a place, system, or person at first mention.

**Repair:** Select what matters now. Add the rest when it changes a decision.

title: Culture or belief as flavor
guidance:
**Tell:** Religion, ritual, identity, or custom appears as decoration without
obligation, authority, practice, disagreement, or cost.

**Repair:** Show what people do, who expects it, who pays, and what happens when
someone refuses.

title: Monster as obstacle
guidance:
**Tell:** Genre fiction or game writing treats a creature only as content to
defeat.

**Repair:** Give it an ecology, appetite, bargain, history, limit, or competing
interest when the world needs that depth.

title: Setting as protagonist service
guidance:
**Tell:** A place or community exists mainly to offer clues, opportunities, or
validation to the protagonist.

**Repair:** Give the setting pressures and routines that continue without the
protagonist.

title: Problem framed as content invitation
guidance:
**Tell:** *This presents an opportunity*, *the party may investigate*, or *the
reader can explore* turns a concrete problem into a packaged activity.

**Repair:** Present the situation, actors, stakes, and worsening pressure. Let the
reader or character choose whether to engage.

title: Sentimental resolution
guidance:
**Tell:** A difficult passage ends with an unearned warm gesture, reassurance, or
claim that everyone will endure.

**Repair:** Let the consequence remain. Use warmth only when a specific action
earned it.

title: Editorial narrative close
guidance:
**Tell:** *And so began...*, *history would remember...*, *the night kept its
secrets*, or *an uncertain future awaited* steps outside the passage to close it.

**Repair:** End on the last action, fact, image, or decision.

title: Repeated weather openings
guidance:
**Tell:** Every scene begins with rain, cold, dawn, darkness, or a lowering sky.

**Repair:** Vary openings among action, dialogue, sound, object, interruption,
claim, and physically experienced weather.

title: Parallel opening-and-ending echo
guidance:
**Tell:** A scene opens and closes on the same image or phrase to create automatic
symmetry.

**Repair:** Let the ending follow what changed. Keep an echo when transformation
of that image is the scene's real structure.

title: Lesson stated directly
guidance:
**Tell:** The close says what the character learned or what the audience should
understand.

**Repair:** Cut the lesson. Strengthen the preceding evidence if the meaning
disappears without it.

title: Flat comma chain
guidance:
**Tell:** Four or more equal-looking units create the appearance of detail without
rank, sequence, or pressure.

**Repair:** Choose the decisive detail, build a sequence, or use a scannable list
when every member matters.

title: Adjective barrage
guidance:
**Tell:** Several labels precede one noun while none identifies a useful material,
condition, scale, ownership, or function.

**Repair:** Keep modifiers that change the reader's image or decision. Put
atmosphere in what the thing does.

title: Pseudo-inventory
guidance:
**Tell:** A room, product, setting, or plan lists plausible components merely to
prove completeness.

**Repair:** Name an item when its condition, owner, use, cost, or absence matters.
Use a real list for a real inventory.

title: Category drift
guidance:
**Tell:** One series treats people, objects, abstractions, causes, and outcomes as
equivalent members.

**Repair:** Separate conceptual kinds. State the material event, then its social
or conceptual consequence.

title: Unordered causal pile
guidance:
**Tell:** Causes or results appear without order, weight, dependency, or a point
where someone can intervene.

**Repair:** Build the chain: cause, response, consequence, current pressure.

title: Example dump
guidance:
**Tell:** A long run of examples substitutes for a rule or representative case.

**Repair:** State the principle and use one revealing example. Group necessary
examples by function.

title: Headless modifier train
guidance:
**Tell:** Multiple qualifications arrive before the reader reaches the noun or
main action.

**Repair:** Put the noun and verb early. Move history, source, and exceptions into
later clauses or sentences.

title: Serial verb chain
guidance:
**Tell:** A character watches, listens, considers, remembers, realizes, and
decides while no visible action changes the scene.

**Repair:** Show the clue and the resulting action. Keep a fast chain when speed
is the point and the last verb changes the situation.

title: Decorative and-chain
guidance:
**Tell:** Repeated *and* lengthens a list without creating labor, panic, ritual,
breath, or speaker-specific rhythm.

**Repair:** Break the sequence into stages and end on failure or decision. Keep
the chain only when its breath pattern does useful work.

title: Parenthetical list inflation
guidance:
**Tell:** A parenthesis, bracket, or dash hides a second catalog after the main
sentence has made its point.

**Repair:** Keep a short necessary example or exception. Give larger sets their
own sentence, list, or table.

title: List as paragraph substitute
guidance:
**Tell:** One sentence or bullet contains several independent procedures,
conditions, outcomes, and exceptions.

**Repair:** Separate trigger, action, result, and exception. Use numbered steps
for real sequences.

title: False completeness
guidance:
**Tell:** *All*, *every*, *comprehensive*, *many aspects*, or an open-ended list
claims mastery the passage does not provide.

**Repair:** State the actual scope. Use *all* only for a closed, defined set.

title: Hedge-stacked prediction
guidance:
**Tell:** A modal stacks with a hedge adverb: *could potentially*, *may
eventually*, *might ultimately*.

**Repair:** Keep one hedge. Make a usable claim. A qualifier that carries a
distinct condition, a different timing, or the writer's confidence stays; a
requested blunt voice is not authority to upgrade a hypothesis to a result.

title: Real or actual adjective inflation
guidance:
**Tell:** *Real*, *actual*, *genuine*, or *true* intensifies an abstract noun
without naming the fake contrast (*real utility*, *genuine tokenomics*). The
word *actually* works the same way as an emphasis-only filler (*this actually
makes the process simpler*). The default fix for *actually* is deletion, not
substitution: just state the fact. Keep *actually* when it marks a specific
correction or expectation gap the sentence names (*we expected a cache hit; it
was actually a miss*), though a direct contrast may still be clearer.

**Repair:** Drop the intensifier and add the specific claim, or name the contrast
explicitly when it is honest.

title: Moral-adjective category error
guidance:
**Tell:** Moral adjectives or adverbs modify non-agent technical nouns (*honest
shape*, *flagged honestly*). Related: assumptions that *stop being true*, or
unverifiable *every* / *all* scope.

**Repair:** Name the concrete property. Prefer *no longer holds*. State real
scope.

title: Invented contrast-pair mirror
guidance:
**Tell:** One half of a pair is a real term of art; the other is a phantom
opposite for symmetry (*false precision rather than genuine accuracy*).

**Repair:** Use a real opposite or state the positive claim alone.

title: Generic future-narrative closer
guidance:
**Tell:** Modal + *become* + *one of the most important narratives / trends /
chapters* with no falsifiable content.

**Repair:** State a checkable prediction or cut the closer.

title: Lingering-attention claim
guidance:
**Tell:** The opener claims duration of attention (*the line I keep coming back
to*, *can't stop thinking about this*) without saying why the thing matters.

**Repair:** Open on the thing itself, or attach the reason.

title: Hashtag stuffing
guidance:
**Tell:** A short post ends with a long block of broad category hashtags
(roughly six or more). The block often mixes one specific tag with empty
category tags (`#AI` `#Innovation` `#FutureTech`).

**Not this tell:** Issue or PR numbers (`#88`), six- or eight-digit hex colours
that include a digit (`#1a2b3c`), C preprocessor lines (`#include`), Markdown
headings, URL fragments, `owner/repo#88`, and anything inside a fence or inline
code span. Short hex-shaped words and channel-style tokens (`#decade`,
`#general`) can still be real tags.

**Repair:** Keep two or three specific tags, or none.

title: Bare noun-phrase bullet list
guidance:
**Tell:** Five or more short adjective-noun bullets with no verbs and no
checkable claim, all the same shape.

**Repair:** Convert to prose or full claims. Leave real inventories, parameters,
changelogs, and todos.

title: Vague third-party validation
guidance:
**Tell:** Unnamed external authority plus superlative (*independent testing
confirms*, *analysts agree we lead*).

**Repair:** Name source, test, and result, or cut the claim.

title: Self-labeling significance
guidance:
**Tell:** After listing items, the prose points back and labels one as
*contrarian*, *clever*, or *the real story*.

**Repair:** Cut the label. Lead with or expand the item that should carry weight.

title: Parenthetical hedge aside
guidance:
**Tell:** Parentheses manufacture nuance without commitment (*(and, increasingly,
Z)*).

**Repair:** Give the aside its own sentence or cut it.

title: Numbered-list inflation
guidance:
**Tell:** *Three key takeaways* or *five things to know* pads content to a round
count.

**Repair:** Keep only discrete parallel items the content earns.

title: Title-case subhead habit
guidance:
**Tell:** Section headings use title case when house style and surrounding text
use sentence case. Same tell on Markdown `#` / `##` lines as on bare title
lines. Ordinary short proper titles and headings that open with *The* are not
the AI section-header habit; the strong form has a mid-title function word
(*And*, *Of*, *For*) across four or more content words
(*Benefits And Strategic Considerations*).

**Repair:** Match house style; default to sentence case for subheads.

title: Historical analogy stack
guidance:
**Tell:** Rapid-fire past technologies or companies borrow weight without
analysis.

**Repair:** Keep one parallel and say what it explains, or cut.

title: Paragraph-reshuffle immunity
guidance:
**Tell:** Body paragraphs can swap order without the reader noticing missing
dependency.

**Repair:** Build a through-line, or make the piece an explicit list.

title: Treadmill restatement
guidance:
**Tell:** A paragraph restates the premise in new words without a new fact,
claim, or turn.

**Repair:** Lead with the new unit or cut the paragraph.

title: Load-bearing metaphor
guidance:
**Tell:** Hyphenated *load-bearing* labels abstract dependencies (*load-bearing
assumption*) outside structural engineering.

**Repair:** Say essential, critical, or what breaks if removed. Keep literal
building uses.

**Boundary:** Flag hyphenated *load-bearing* only when it immediately modifies
*assumption*, *claim*, *invariant*, *premise*, *constraint*, *dependency*,
*argument*, or *abstraction* (including plurals). Unhyphenated *load bearing*
is ordinary English. Unlisted nouns, intervening modifiers, mixed
physical-or-abstract nouns (*structure*, *element*, *frame*, *foundation*),
and predicative uses (*the wall is load-bearing*) pass. This deliberately
misses some metaphors to avoid flagging ordinary writing. (Adapted from
avoid-ai-writing v3.33.0, MIT.)

title: Narrated candor
guidance:
**Tell:** The prose announces its own disclosure instead of disclosing:
*Two caveats I would rather flag than let you discover later*, *I want to be
upfront*, *To be fully transparent*, *Rather than bury this, I'll say it
plainly*, *I could have left this out, but*, *Being honest about the
limitations here*. The content is often only *Two caveats:*; the rest advertises
the writer's forthrightness. Often arrives as a matched antithesis (*flag*
rather than *let you discover*).

This sits with chatbot helpfulness performance and sycophantic reader-flattery:
those perform helpfulness or praise; this performs candor about oneself.

**Repair:** Cut the frame. State the caveat, limit, or fact. Deletion test: if
cutting the frame loses no information, it was never content.

**Carve-outs:** Keep substantive admissions (*I haven't tested this on
Windows*, *this is a mitigation, not a fix*). Keep conventional conflict-of-
interest openings that carry a material fact (*In the interest of full
disclosure, I own shares in the company discussed here*). Ordinary comparatives
about work are not this pattern (*I'd rather fix it than let you inherit the
mess*). The empty frame with nothing behind it still counts.

Judgment-only: the same words appear in idiomatic disclosure language. Decide
whether the clause carries information or only announces that information is
coming.

title: False agency
guidance:
**Tell:** An inanimate or abstract subject performs a human verb: *the
complaint becomes a fix*, *a bet lives or dies*, *the decision emerges*, *the
culture shifts*, *the conversation moves toward*, *the data tells us*, *the
market rewards*. AI leans on this because it avoids naming the actor.

**Repair:** Name the human. *The team fixed it that week* beats *the complaint
becomes a fix*. If no specific person fits, use *you* to put the reader in the
seat. (Adapted from hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

Judgment-only P2: flag an obscured accountable decision-maker, as in *the
decision emerged after the offsite* with no decider named. Apply only when a
specific person or team exercised judgment and naming them matters to the
passage. Name the actor only when the source identifies them; otherwise ask
who decided instead of inventing a decider. Preserve conventional
personification (*the data shows adoption is early*), literal system behavior,
collective shorthand (*the market rewards shipping*), emergent change (*the
culture shifted*), and causal dependence (*a bet lives or dies on
distribution*). A consequential choice attributed to an abstraction, with its
responsible actor missing, still flags. (P2 extension adapted from
avoid-ai-writing v3.33.0, MIT.)

title: Wh- opener crutch
guidance:
**Tell:** Sentences start with *What, When, Where, Which, Who, Why,* or *How*
as an announcement scaffold: *What makes this hard is...*, *Why this matters
is...*, *How we fix it is...*. The question word defers the subject.

**Repair:** Lead with the subject or verb. *What makes this hard is the
approval chain* → *The approval chain is the hard part*. Paragraphs starting
with *So* and sentences starting with *Look,* are the same tic. (Adapted from
hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

title: Negative-listing buildup
guidance:
**Tell:** The writer lists what something is *not* before revealing what it
*is*: *Not a dashboard... Not a portal... A single page.* Or *It wasn't X. It
wasn't Y. It was Z.* A rhetorical striptease that delays the point.

**Repair:** State Z directly. The reader does not need the runway. Distinct
from pattern 9 (single negative-then-positive) in that the buildup runs
multiple negations. (Adapted from hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

title: Staccato fragmentation
guidance:
**Tell:** Sentence fragments stacked for emphasis: *[Noun]. That's it. That's
the [thing].* / *X. And Y. And Z.* / *This unlocks something. [Word].*
Manufactured profundity.

**Repair:** Complete sentences, and trust content over presentation. One
fragment can carry real emphasis; a run of them is a rhythm tell. (Adapted from
hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

title: Unnecessary hyphenation
guidance:
**Tell:** Three subtypes. Welded open noun phrases are hyphenated when the
standard form is open (*research-impact aggregator* becomes *research impact
aggregator*). Compounds whose established form is closed keep the hyphen by
mistake (*code-base* becomes *codebase*, *data-set* becomes *dataset*).
Attributive compounds used adverbially or as nouns keep the hyphen where it
does not belong (*in real-time* becomes *in real time*), while the same compound
before a noun stays hyphenated (*real-time analytics* is correct).

**Repair:** Treat a clear hit as P2 copyediting, not evidence of machine
authorship. Preserve established and technical compounds (*high-quality*,
*third-party*, *family-owned*). Spelling varies by dialect and house style, so
ambiguous pairs are judgment calls. Predicative after the noun stays open
(*the report is high quality*). Hyphenate attributive-before-noun only.

title: Shadowboxing objections
guidance:
**Tell:** The text answers an objection nobody raised: *This isn't mainly about
X*, *I'm not arguing that Y*, *To be clear*, *Don't get me wrong*, *You could
frame this differently, but*, *Some might say... but*. The named objection
appears nowhere else and nobody in the text holds it.

**Repair:** Remove the unsupported defense. If it contains a real claim, state
that claim directly. Keep an objection when the text names its source or answers
it in full; a direct claim such as *the API is not thread-safe* is not this
pattern. (Adapted from blader/humanizer, MIT.)

title: Editorial scar tissue
guidance:
**Tell:** The draft still records the writer's earlier drafting choices: *A
tempting approach would be to... but*, *One might be tempted to*, *An obvious
approach would be*, *You might think... but*, *It would be easy to just*, *Some
would suggest*. An option no reader would consider gets introduced and rejected
in a clause, then never appears again. Several short unrelated rejections in one
passage are a stronger sign than one.

**Repair:** Remove the fake option and state the real constraint or current
behavior directly. Ask what new information each sentence adds; if it only
records an earlier edit, rewrite the paragraph around its main point. Keep real
alternatives a reader may genuinely weigh in a design doc, tutorial, or
argument. (Adapted from blader/humanizer, MIT.)

title: Rhetorical setup
guidance:
**Tell:** The text announces insight instead of delivering it: *What if [the
problem is really X]?*, *Here's what I mean:*, *Think about it:*, *And that's
okay.* A Socratic question, redundant preview, condescending prompt, or
permission-granting tagline precedes a point that could stand alone. The
question is answered immediately, every time.

**Repair:** Make the point. Cut the scaffold and let readers draw the
conclusion. A genuine open question that the piece later answers with evidence
is not this pattern; the tell is the setup that exists only to stage the
answer. (Adapted from hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

title: Narrator from a distance
guidance:
**Tell:** The prose floats above the scene: *Nobody designed this.*, *This
happens because...*, *This is why...*, *People tend to...*. A disembodied
observer describes behavior in general instead of putting the reader in the
room where it happens.

**Repair:** Put the reader in the scene. *You don't sit down one day and decide
to write sloppy* beats *Nobody designed this*. Where general statement is the
actual job (a spec, a summary), keep it; the tell is floating voice used where
specifics would carry more. (Adapted from hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

title: Announced significance
guidance:
**Tell:** The text asserts its own difficulty or importance instead of showing
it: *This is genuinely hard*, *This is what leadership actually looks like*,
*This is what X actually looks like*, *actually matters*. Telling instead of
showing, in the register of profundity.

**Repair:** Cut the announcement. Show the hard part or the example. If the
claim survives only because the announcement is there, the passage was not
carrying it. (Adapted from hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

title: Additive hedge escalation
guidance:
**Tell:** Escalating additive constructions: *not just X but also Y*, *not
merely X but Y*, *X isn't only Y, it's Z*. The negation inflates the second
item by pretending the first was ever in question.

**Repair:** State Y (or both items) directly. Distinct from pattern 9
(negative-then-positive contrast): the additive hedge stacks items rather than
correcting a real misconception. Keep genuine two-part scope (*not just the
client, the server too*) when both halves are load-bearing facts. (Adapted from hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

title: Template narrative arc
guidance:
**Tell:** Prefab story templates carry the paragraph: *By the time X, I was
Y*, *It started with... It ended with...*, *At first... Then...*. The arc does
real narrative work the writer did not do; events slot into a shape that
arrived before them.

**Repair:** Report the events in their own order and let the sequence carry
the arc. Keep the template when the events genuinely follow it and the shape
is not doing the persuading. (Adapted from hardikpandya/stop-slop, MIT.)

title: Performed insight
guidance:
**Tell:** Essayist tics that announce profundity instead of delivering it:
*sit with that for a moment*, *that's not nothing*, *you already know the
answer*, *the punchline is*, *worth naming*, *don't take my word for it*,
*that's the whole point*, *is the entire business model*, *that's the part
nobody mentions*, *the only metric that matters*, *X is dead; long live X*,
and sentence-initial *Turns out*. Each stages a reveal; none adds a fact.

**Repair:** State the claim the phrase was gesturing at. *That's not nothing*
becomes the actual size of the thing; *the punchline is* becomes the point,
unannounced.

**Carve-outs:** One hit can be a stylistic choice; several in one piece is the
tell. Quoted speech and genuinely comedic writing keep literal punchlines.
Staged-discovery variants such as *it turned out to be the least interesting
part* and *the real story was that...* use the same reveal frame; revise them
when the phrasing supplies drama without new information. Keep literal outcomes
such as *it turned out to be the most expensive option* and literal reports such
as *the real story was covered yesterday*. An essay title, a supported contrast,
or a literal succession announcement in *X is dead; long live Y* form names the
argument, so judge whether the wording substitutes for one rather than flagging
the phrase. (Adapted from avoid-ai-writing v3.28.0, v3.36.0, and v3.38.0, MIT;
source: Simon Willison's LLM cliché highlighter.)

title: Negation chain
guidance:
**Tell:** A drumroll of negations performing decisiveness: *No fluff, no
filler, no jargon*, stacked *didn't ... didn't* clauses (*It didn't ask, it
didn't wait*), and the negated-then-repeated verb (*Don't call it a pivot.
Call it a correction*). Extends pattern 76 (negative-listing buildup); the
chain form is the rhetorical drumroll even without fragment shaping.

**Repair:** Say what the thing is. One negation earns its place when the reader
would otherwise assume the opposite; a chain of them is staging.

**Carve-outs:** Mid-sentence factual inventories (*takes no arguments, no
headers, and no body*) and sequential narration with restated subjects (*I did
not sleep well. I did not eat breakfast.*) are ordinary prose. (Adapted from
avoid-ai-writing, MIT.)

title: Dev-blog boilerplate
guidance:
**Tell:** Stock simplicity slogans from developer marketing: *batteries
included*, *it just works*, *zero config*, *sane defaults*, *small enough to
fit in your head*. Each substitutes a slogan for a property you could
demonstrate.

**Repair:** Name the concrete behavior. *Installs with no config file* beats
*zero config*; *the whole API is six functions* beats *fits in your head*.

**Carve-outs:** Quoting a product's own tagline or discussing the phrase
itself. (Adapted from avoid-ai-writing, MIT.)

title: Stacked rhetorical questions
guidance:
**Tell:** Two or more questions fired in a row, usually fragments after the
first: *Do I know how it works? Where it breaks? Which corners it cut?* A
performance of curiosity, not a real question. Extends pattern 81 (rhetorical
setup) to the chain form.

**Repair:** Keep at most one question, answer it, and convert the rest into the
statements they were hiding.

**Carve-outs:** Interviews, FAQs, and dialogue stack questions legitimately.
(Adapted from avoid-ai-writing, MIT.)

title: Same-opener sentence runs
guidance:
**Tell:** Three or more consecutive sentences opening on the same word (*Maybe
nobody needed it. Maybe it solved the wrong problem. Maybe the timing was
off.*), or consecutive sentences on one repeated skeleton. Deliberate anaphora
is a rhetorical device; a run that is not doing persuasive work is a tell.

**Repair:** Keep the first, vary or merge the rest.

**Carve-outs:** Whether the repetition is earned is the judgment; pronoun-opener
runs (*He... He... He...*) are ordinary narration. (Adapted from
avoid-ai-writing, MIT.)

title: Stranded auxiliary contrast
guidance:
**Tell:** A reversal landed on a bare auxiliary: *The tool died; the data
didn't.* One instance is a fine sentence; as a recurring rhythm it is a
signature move, and the clipped contrast poses as earned insight.

**Repair:** Ration it. If the piece already has one, write the next contrast
out in full.

**Carve-outs:** The single deliberate instance is legitimate style; only
density across a piece distinguishes voice from tic. (Adapted from
avoid-ai-writing, MIT.)

title: Colon into a triple
guidance:
**Tell:** A colon opening onto exactly three comma-separated items: *separate
ports, processes, and local state*. The default rhythm LLM prose uses to sound
concrete, whether or not the content has three parts.

**Repair:** Audit the list. If there are really two things, or four, write
that; if the items are padding, cut to the one that matters.

**Carve-outs:** Three-item lists are often simply true, especially in technical
writing. Weigh by genre, not per hit. (Adapted from avoid-ai-writing, MIT.)

title: Launch-copy dramatic introductions
guidance:
**Tell:** The default LLM move for product and launch posts: *Enter Flowdesk*,
*Meet Flowdesk, your new favorite treasury dashboard*, *Say hello to Flowdesk*,
*Think Notion meets Figma*. The product is introduced like a game-show
contestant instead of being described. Sits next to the stale social-ad tells
(unlock, elevate, link in bio), but no other entry names the introduction move
itself.

**Repair:** Say what the thing does and for whom. *Meet Flowdesk, your new
favorite treasury dashboard* becomes *Flowdesk shows a fund's full treasury
position on one screen*.

**Carve-outs:** Bare *Enter X* is how UI and documentation instructions are
written (*Enter Password.*) and how dramatic scripts mark stage entrances, so it
flags only in launch and announcement copy, by judgment. Bare *Meet X, your new
[role]* is how humans introduce colleagues, pets, and babies. *Say hello to X*
covers ordinary human prose. (Adapted from avoid-ai-writing v3.29.0, MIT.)

title: Fake-casual register
guidance:
**Tell:** The register models emit when asked for a lowercase-casual social
voice, once the vocabulary tiers are clean: one-word verdict closers as the
whole closing line (*wild.*, *insane.*), stage directions (*checks notes*,
*chef's kiss*, *mic drop*), wink asides *(yes, really)*, label-prefix openers
(*hot take*, *fun fact*, *pro tip*, *PSA*, *unpopular opinion*), *because of
course it does*, and the self-QA volley (*Is it fast? Yes. Is it cheap? Also
yes*). The drama is outsourced to the prop instead of carried by the content,
which is why it survives cleanup.

**Repair:** Delete the label and say the thing. Replace the verdict word with
the specific surprise. Cut the wink and the stage business.

**Carve-outs:** A writer whose established voice runs on these props keeps
them; the register is a tell for imposed casualness, not a ban on playfulness.
The deterministic detector covers only the mechanical props (six stage
directions, four parentheticals, both closed lists). (Adapted from
avoid-ai-writing v3.29.0, MIT.)

title: Dramatized contrast against the crowd
guidance:
**Tell:** A claim propped on an invented lagging crowd, usually stamped with a
date: *shipped it in 2022, while everyone else was still debating timelines*,
*built it in a weekend, while the industry wrote think-pieces*. The crowd is
invented, so the contrast costs nothing. Adjacent to significance inflation and
self-labeling significance, but the surface is its own: the trailing *while
everyone else...* clause with a dismissive verb.

**Repair:** State the fact and cut the crowd clause, or name the actual
competitor and what they did. If the crowd cannot be named, it was invented.

**Carve-outs:** Literal simultaneity is ordinary narrative and stays
unflagged: *she read while everyone else watched the movie*. The deterministic
branch requires the dismissive verb in its -ing form plus *still*; the other
two branches match their own stereotyped wording (*wrote think-pieces*,
*played catch-up*). (Adapted from avoid-ai-writing v3.29.0, MIT.)

title: Transformation crutch
guidance:
**Tell:** Repeated unexplained relabeling across a passage: *the concern turns
into panic*, *a feature turns into a strategy*, *the risk becomes real*. The
passage asserts a change without the action, threshold, or consequence that
would make it one.

**Repair:** Ask what changed and read the surrounding passage before deciding
the explanation is missing. Rewrite from supplied facts; never invent a
mechanism or actor. If the explanation was already present elsewhere, leave
the sentence alone.

**Carve-outs:** Literal transformations (*water turns into ice*), supported
metaphors, and changes explained anywhere in the passage pass, including
deliberate summaries of explained changes. Judgment-only P2, not authorship
evidence. (Adapted from avoid-ai-writing v3.31.0, MIT.)

title: Consequence-free restatement
guidance:
**Tell:** *This matters because* or *here is why that matters* introduces a
restatement of importance rather than a reason: *This matters because it is
important.* The frame promises stakes and delivers the premise again. Same
family: a sentence after an example that names what the example showed
(*This shows the importance of...*, *The message was clear:*, *It was a
lesson in patience.*).

**Repair:** Cut the empty frame, or replace it with an explanation already
present in the source. Never invent stakes. Preserve the frame when a concrete
consequence follows (*This matters because retries can charge the customer
twice*). Judgment-only P2 clarity check. (Adapted from avoid-ai-writing
v3.31.0, MIT.)

title: Repeated empty concessions
guidance:
**Tell:** Concession pairs staged to sound honest without saying where the
claim fails: *Not always. Not perfectly.* repeated across a passage. One
honest hedge becomes a rhythm of performed humility.

**Repair:** Fold repeated empty concessions into a limitation already stated
in the source, or cut them. Keep every supplied assessment and limitation; a
generic-sounding concession is still the writer's claim. Never invent a failure
case or drop a stated assessment because its wording is ordinary.

**Carve-outs:** Meaningful concessions (*Not during failover. Not for expired
tokens*) and an isolated intentional pair pass. Judgment-only P2. (Adapted
from avoid-ai-writing v3.31.0, MIT.)

title: Repeated setup/reversal punchlines
guidance:
**Tell:** Two or more paraprosdokian reversals in one piece, especially in
hooks, closers, or final list items: each sentence sets an expectation in its
first half and flips it in the second, so repeated flips replace concrete
claims with generic surprise or deflation. This concerns setup and payoff
across sentences; pattern 77 covers runs of same-shape fragments.

**Repair:** Keep at most one reversal and give the rest concrete claims. A
repair must not shrink the supplied scope: *We planned for every failure mode.
Except the one that happened* becomes *We planned for every failure mode except
the one that happened*, not a generic admission that one was missed. Treat as a
clarity and rhythm edit, not proof of authorship.

**Carve-outs:** Supported reversals, isolated intentional lines, and genuine
comedy, fiction, speeches, and quotations pass. Repetition alone is not a
finding. Judgment-only P2. (Adapted from avoid-ai-writing v3.30.0, MIT.)

title: Vague association
guidance:
**Tell:** *associated with*, *linked to*, *in connection with* with no named
relationship.

**Repair:** Use the relationship the source names. If it names none, keep the
vague wording. Do not invent a CEO, consultant, or role to sound concrete.

title: Empty concession sandwich
guidance:
**Tell:** *While X is impressive, Y remains a challenge* when both halves are
vague. A lone pair is ordinary prose. The tell is repetition, and the vague close
has to sit in a later clause of the same sentence.

**Repair:** Specify both halves, or keep the supplied assessment and flag the
scope it leaves unstated; the writer's positive or negative judgment is source
meaning, not filler to choose between. Distinct from empty "Not always. Not
perfectly." (Assessment carve-out from the avoid-ai-writing post-v3.38.0 tip,
MIT.)

title: Significance-adverb density
guidance:
**Tell:** *Notably*, *Interestingly*, *Importantly*, *Significantly* as a
run, not a single hit.

**Repair:** Treat as a density tell. One in a long piece can stay. Several in
a short piece go. Replace the survivor with the fact.

title: Parallel reason chains
guidance:
**Tell:** Three or more consecutive `subject + because/when + reason`.

**Repair:** Break the chain. Vary the join.

title: Intensifier / diminisher opposition
guidance:
**Tell:** *X obsessively / Y barely at all* as a fake contrast engine.

**Repair:** State the actual difference without the theatrical poles.

title: Participial reframe
guidance:
**Tell:** *Laid out that way*, *Seen this way*, *Put differently* as a
throat-clear before the real sentence.

**Repair:** Start at the claim.

title: Hedged-enumeration openers
guidance:
**Tell:** *There are several ways to*, *a few things to consider*, *It is
generally a good idea to*.

**Repair:** Answer first. Drop the throat-clear.

title: Re-explaining what the reader knows
guidance:
**Tell:** In a reply, the answer rebuilds context the reader already has: it
restates the problem, walks the diagnosis, lays out the evidence, and reaches
the decision in the last line. Each sentence reads fine on its own, which is
why the shape survives sentence-level cleanup. Related: pasting a query,
command, or numbers to prove the plan will work; re-walking background the
other person wrote or agreed to.

**Repair:** Lead with the decision. Keep only the reasoning that would change
whether the reader agrees: usually one fact they lack and any link they need
to act. The diagnosis and the proof belong in the ticket or document that
follows. A reviewer raising a topic is not a request for the full write-up.

**Carve-outs:** Act when the surrounding conversation is visible or the text
is plainly a reply; when you cannot tell, ask or leave the text alone. A
standalone document for readers with no shared context is exempt, and one
line of framing in a long thread is ordinary. (Adapted from blader/humanizer
v3.1.0 §26, MIT.)

title: Mannered prose
guidance:
**Tell:** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists. Figurative verbs
(*rides along*, *stands on*), personified code (*the plan holds it*),
aphoristic fragments (*wire it or delete it*), and stock framing phrases.
*A dial worth turning* says *a parameter worth varying* with less clarity.

**Repair:** Say what you mean. Check the sentence for a literal equivalent and
use it; keep the image when it carries real meaning a plainer phrase would
lose.

**Carve-outs:** Not the same as pattern 72, which covers only the hyphenated
*load-bearing* label, and not the secondary-cleanup aphorism formula. Sustained
metaphor that organizes a whole passage is a writer's chosen device; flag the
isolated flourish. (Adapted from cursor/plugins unslop, MIT.)

title: Over-compression
guidance:
**Tell:** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and unexplained
abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read: *Parser rejects bad
date → exit 2, no write*.

**Repair:** Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out
arrows and abbreviations.

**Carve-outs:** Recognized shorthand in code comments, console transcripts,
changelogs, and dense tables can stay when the audience already reads it that
way; that is a register judgment, not a defect. Related to pattern 77, which
repairs the same habit in the opposite direction. (Adapted from
cursor/plugins unslop, MIT.)

title: Stock reaction frame
guidance:
**Tell:** A stock introduction carries the writer's stance instead of a fact:
*What surprised me most was...*, *The most interesting part...*, *What I love
about this is...*. The frame is soft; the judgment inside it is the writer's.

**Repair:** Cut the frame when the supplied fact already carries its whole
meaning, and rephrase only while keeping the reaction, preference, or ranking.
A stated judgment stands as source meaning even when its reason is missing, so
never drop it, and never trade a named emotion for theatrical body language to
satisfy *show, don't tell*. Add an expectation or a cause only when the source
supplies one.

**Carve-outs:** Fiction, deliberate rhetorical openings, and frames whose
preference is stated elsewhere in the source pass. When the judgment cannot be
reconstructed safely, keep it and report the gap. (Adapted from the
avoid-ai-writing post-v3.38.0 tip, MIT.)
